commitResults.messageTitle: Merge A-Jar
Docs: Document command constructors and details
commitResults.messageBody:
Commands.java holds the command factory and every concrete command
class, but only the classes and execute methods carried header
comments. The constructors and the shared details field were left
undocumented, so a reader could not tell what each constructor
expects without tracing back through Parser.

Add a header comment to every command constructor stating which part
of the user input its details argument carries, document the shared
InputCommand.details field, and note why the Commands factory has a
private constructor.

This covers the package-private declarations in this file, which the
javadoc tool does not report on but the stretch goal still requires.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document command keyword constants
commitResults.messageBody:
The CommandType enum lists the ten keywords Nori recognises, but the
constants themselves carried no header comments. The keyword strings
alone do not say what each command does, so the generated API docs
listed ten undocumented constants.

Add a single-line header comment to each constant describing the
behaviour it selects, which is the level of detail the coding
standard allows for class members.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document the implicit class constructors
commitResults.messageBody:
Command and Parser both relied on Java's implicit default
constructor, which cannot carry a header comment. The javadoc tool
reported both as undocumented, and neither constructor is meant to
be called: Command is abstract, and Parser only exposes static
methods.

Declare each constructor explicitly so it can be documented, and
narrow Parser's to private. Parser is never instantiated anywhere in
the project, so this removes an accidental public constructor from
the API and matches how the Commands factory is already written.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document task display representations
commitResults.messageBody:
Every task class overrides toString to build the exact text the user
sees in a task list, and each subclass adds its own type icon and
detail suffix. None of the four overrides carried a header comment,
so the only way to learn the display format of a task was to read
the string concatenation.

Document each override with the shape of the string it returns, so
the format the UI and the regression tests depend on is stated in
one place per task type.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document storage file and recovery fields
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage keeps seven separate paths and two pieces of recovery state.
Names such as corruptFilePath, legacyBackupFilePath and
canWriteToStorage do not say when each one is used, so the save and
recovery logic had to be read end to end before the field list made
sense.

Add a single-line header comment to each field naming its role in
the save, backup, recovery and legacy-migration paths. The agent
guidelines ask for header comments on fields whose purpose is not
obvious, and these fields are the least obvious in the project.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document regression test helpers
commitResults.messageBody:
The two regression suites document their test scenarios but not the
harness underneath them. runTest, the runNori launchers, the cleanup
helpers and the hand-written assertions had no header comments, even
though the three runNori variants differ only in how they point Nori
at its storage directory, which is exactly the detail a reader needs.

Document each helper and both test-case interfaces, stating what the
runNori variants do differently. The test methods themselves stay
undocumented: their names already follow the
scenario_condition_expectedBehaviour form, and the coding standard
exempts test methods from header comments.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document the no-argument command constructors
commitResults.messageBody:
HelpCommand, ExitCommand and UnknownCommand take no details, so each
relied on Java's implicit default constructor. An implicit
constructor cannot carry a header comment, and javadoc reported all
three when run at private visibility.

Declare the three constructors explicitly with a header comment
each, matching the treatment already given to Command and Parser.
Every constructor in the command package is now documented.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document remaining fields and constants
commitResults.messageBody:
Running javadoc at private visibility showed that while every class
and method now had a header comment, most fields did not. Some are
self-evident, but several are not: Event's DATE_PATTERN, Deadline's
DISPLAY_FORMATTER, the /by and /from separators, and Nori's pair of
loadingError and loadingNotice fields.

Document every remaining field with a single-line header comment so
the whole of src/main/java reports zero javadoc warnings at private
visibility. The agent guidelines ask for comments on fields whose
purpose is not obvious; documenting the few obvious ones alongside
them keeps the rule easy to check rather than a judgement call.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Mandate the Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The seedu-java-coding-standard skill records the rules but nothing
tells an agent to load it, so it would only be used when someone
remembered to ask. The standard has to apply to every Java change in
this project from this increment onward, including code written in
later increments.

Add a Java coding standard section to the project requirements that
requires the skill to be invoked before any Java file is written,
edited, or reviewed, and states that non-compliant code is not
finished work.

Also say what to do with existing non-compliant code found in
passing: fix it when the fix is small and in scope, otherwise leave
it and report it, so following the standard does not silently widen
the scope of unrelated changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Mandate the Git commit standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The Git section of the project requirements asks for enough detail to
explain a change, but says nothing about the form of the message. The
seedu-git-standard skill now records that form and needs to be
reachable the same way the coding standard is.

Require the skill to be invoked before any commit message is proposed
or written, and keep the existing lightweight-tag rule and the rule
against committing unless asked, which the SE-EDU convention does not
cover.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Parenthesise the command keyword match
commitResults.messageBody:
findCommandType decides whether an input line starts a command by
combining an exact keyword match with a prefix match, written as
`a || b && c` across a wrapped line. The condition is correct only
because && binds tighter than ||, so a reader has to recall the
precedence rule to check it, and the wrapped line ran to 112
characters.

Name the two halves as isExactMatch and isPrefixMatch and test them
separately. The coding standard asks for explicit grouping when && and
|| are mixed, requires boolean names to carry an is prefix, and sets a
110 character soft limit, and the named form satisfies all three.

Both operands are side-effect free, so evaluating the prefix match
eagerly rather than short-circuiting cannot change behaviour.

Add three Parser tests covering the branch this touches: a keyword
without its separating space, a non-bye keyword followed by details,
and a bare keyword yielding empty details.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Rename the date match boolean
commitResults.messageBody:
getMatchingTasks holds the result of its date test in a local called
matches. The coding standard requires boolean names to be prefixed
with is, has, was or similar, and a bare verb reads as an action
rather than a state.

Rename the local to isMatch. This is the only boolean in the project
that did not already carry such a prefix; the predicate methods named
occursOn, occursInDateRange and containsDate are left as they are,
since each already reads as a boolean question at its call site.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Wrap main source lines under 110 columns
commitResults.messageBody:
Six lines in the main source ran between 111 and 117 characters. The
coding standard sets a 110 character soft limit with 120 as the hard
limit, so these were legal but over the limit the project aims for.

Wrap each one, breaking after a comma or before a + operator and
indenting the continuation by 8 spaces, as the standard prescribes.
Two of the six are user-facing message literals that had to be split
across a concatenation, which changes the source without changing the
string.

One of those two, the message shown when saved tasks and their backup
are both unreadable, had no test asserting it. Add a storage
regression case that corrupts the storage file and its backup
together, so the split literal is checked rather than assumed
correct.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Wrap test source lines under 110 columns
commitResults.messageBody:
Twenty-four lines across the two regression suites ran between 111
and 120 characters, mostly test registrations in main and assertions
carrying long expected strings.

Wrap each one, breaking after a comma and indenting the continuation
by 8 spaces. No expression is restructured and no expected string is
altered, so every case still asserts exactly what it asserted before.

Reword one Javadoc summary in StorageTest that was a single 116
character sentence, rather than splitting it mid-clause.

commitResults.messageTitle: Feat: Add keyword search to the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
A user with a long list has no way to pull out the tasks that mention
a particular thing; the only queries are by date. Level 9 asks for a
search over the task description.

Add getTasksMatchingKeywordDisplayLines, which returns display lines
for every task whose description contains the keyword, alongside the
existing date queries and reusing their heading helper.

Three decisions worth recording:

- The search is case insensitive and matches anywhere in the
  description, so "book" finds both "read book" and "Bookshop
  errand". Case folding uses Locale.ROOT so the result does not
  depend on the machine's locale.
- Only the description is searched. A deadline's date and an event's
  start and end are not, which is what "keyword in the task
  description" asks for and keeps find distinct from on and list.
- Matching lines keep their numbers from the full list rather than
  being renumbered from 1, so a number shown by find can be passed
  straight to mark, unmark or delete. This matches what on and list
  already do.

Add a TaskListTest covering both, empty and non-matching searches,
case folding, a mid-word match, and the task numbering.

commitResults.messageTitle: Feat: Add the find command
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list can now search itself by keyword, but nothing reaches
that search from user input.

Add FIND to the command keywords and a FindCommand that passes the
text after the keyword to the list's keyword search. The whole
remainder of the line is the keyword, so "find return book" searches
for the phrase rather than for either word.

Guard the empty case. A bare "find" would otherwise match every task,
since every description contains the empty string, which is a
confusing answer to an obvious mistake. Report it the way the other
commands report missing details, with ui.showResponse rather than an
exception, so find behaves like todo does with no description.

Add Parser cases for a single-word keyword, a multi-word keyword, a
bare find, and the "finder" prefix that must not be treated as find.

commitResults.messageTitle: Feat: List find in the help text
commitResults.messageBody:
The help command is where a user learns what Nori understands, so a
command missing from it is effectively undiscoverable. find was
missing.

Add "find <keyword>" between the list and mark entries, keeping the
help order the same as the command keyword order.

Update the two places that assert the full help output: the expected
output of the help case in the UI test plan, and the help regression
test. Both are expectation updates for a deliberate addition, not
loosened assertions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Cover find end to end
commitResults.messageBody:
The unit tests exercise the keyword search directly, but nothing ran
find through a real Nori session, where the command wiring, the empty
keyword guard and the console formatting all have to line up.

Add a regression case and a UI test plan case, both driving one
session that searches for a missing keyword, an upper-case keyword
against lower-case descriptions, and a lower-case keyword against a
capitalised description, then a bare find.

Searching both directions is deliberate. An earlier version of this
case searched only an upper-case keyword, which folds the keyword but
never the description, so a search that stopped folding descriptions
still passed. Covering both directions closes that gap: reverting
either half of the case folding now fails this case.

The expected output in the test plan is a recorded session rather
than transcribed by hand, so it cannot drift from what Nori prints.

The command factory's case labels use the wrong indentation.

Feat: Expose commands to graphical UI
commitResults.messageBody:
Nori's command loop is tied to console input and output, which
prevents a graphical controller from reusing the application logic.

Add an injectable UI boundary and a single-command execution method so
both console and JavaFX front ends share the same parser, task list,
storage, and error handling.

commitResults.messageTitle: Feat: Add JavaFX chat interface
commitResults.messageBody:
Nori has no graphical interface, so desktop users can interact with it
only through a terminal.

Add the tutorial-aligned JavaFX dependencies, Launcher entry point, FXML
views, styled chat controls, and bundled penguin visuals. Keep dependencies
for all three supported operating systems so Gradle builds stay portable.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Explain JavaFX application workflow
commitResults.messageBody:
The project documentation still describes the console starter template and
does not explain how to launch or package the JavaFX application.

Document the Gradle, IDE, and executable JAR workflows. Ignore the local
Pingu reference folder while retaining only the optimized bundled asset.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix: Validate dated event intervals
commitResults.messageBody:
Dated events accept reversed endpoints and an on-date query checks only the
two endpoints, so multi-day events disappear on intermediate dates.

Reject reversed dated intervals and treat both endpoints as an inclusive
span. Add boundary, undated, persistence, oversized-index, and hostile-text
JUnit cases to protect command and storage behavior.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Cover event and hostile input scenarios
commitResults.messageBody:
The console UI plan does not cover intermediate dates in multi-day events,
reversed endpoints, or input that resembles markup, paths, and shell text.

Add exact-output sessions for those cases so future changes must preserve
chronological validation, inclusive matching, and literal data handling.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-10
Feat: Add varargs task list construction
commitResults.messageBody:
Callers that already hold individual tasks must first wrap them in a list
before constructing a TaskList.

Add a Task varargs constructor for concise fixed-size call sites. Delegate to
the existing list constructor so the supplied argument array is not retained.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Cover varargs task construction
commitResults.messageBody:
The new varargs constructor needs protection against argument reordering and
accidental retention of the caller's mutable array.

Use the overload in the sample fixture and test ordered arguments, empty
arguments, and defensive array copying.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Varargs
Docs: Add a conventions folder for SE-EDU guides
commitResults.messageBody:
The conventions this project follows exist only as links to
se-education.org, spread across AGENTS.md and two agent skills. A
contributor has to open four web pages to learn the rules, and nothing
records which of the choices those guides leave open this project has
made.

Links also rot silently. When an upstream page changes there is no diff
to review, so the project drifts from the standard without anyone
noticing.

Let's check a working copy of each guide into docs/conventions, one file
per guide, with the choices this project has committed to stated inline.

A checked-in copy makes the rules reviewable: a change to the standard
now arrives as a pull request diff like any other change. The upstream
pages stay the authority, so every file names its source and the README
says to update the local copy when a page changes.

Covers the git, Java, logging and Checkstyle guides, plus the guide
index at https://se-education.org/guides/.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Point agent instructions at docs/conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md states the coding and commit rules by linking out to
se-education.org, and tells the reader to invoke a skill for each one.

That duplicates what docs/conventions now holds, and leaves two places
that can disagree about the same rule.

Let's make AGENTS.md name docs/conventions as the authoritative copy and
index the files in a table, so a reader knows which one covers the task
in front of them.

The skills carry the same rules and stay usable, so this changes only
which source is named first. A logging section is added because the
project had no written guidance on logging at all, and a Checkstyle
command is named because the rule it enforces was previously stated
without saying how to check it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Feat: Give Nori a penguin persona
commitResults.messageBody:
Nori's console messages read as generic assistant text, with a few
Singlish asides such as "lah" and "sia" mixed into some of them. The
voice shifts between commands, and none of it says anything about Nori
itself.

A task tracker is used many times a day, so its responses are most of
what a user ever sees of it. A steady, recognisable voice makes the app
pleasant to come back to; a mixed one makes it feel unfinished.

Let's give Nori one persona, a small penguin, and rewrite every console
message in that voice. Errors open with "NOOT?!", confirmations with
"Noot noot!", and the task list becomes an iceberg.

One persona is chosen over per-command tone because these messages are
read in sequence within a single session, where a shift in voice reads
as a bug rather than as variety.

Two wording problems are corrected while rewriting:

* "Now you have 1 tasks in the list" becomes a "task(s)" form that is
  correct for every count
* each message names the command it concerns and shows a working
  example, so a user is never left guessing what to type next

commitResults.messageTitle: Feat: Reword the GUI shell in Nori's penguin voice
commitResults.messageBody:
Nori's console messages now speak as a penguin, but the JavaFX shell
around them keeps the old wording: an "A calm place for busy days"
tagline, a "Ready to help" status pill and a "Session complete"
farewell.

Half an interface in one voice and half in another reads as an
oversight, and the greeting is the first thing a new user sees.

Let's reword the greeting, tagline, status pill and exit message to
match the console persona.

Decorative text takes the persona; functional text does not. The input
prompt, the send button, its accessible label and the keyboard hint keep
plain wording, because a user reading those is working out what to type
or what a control does. The accessible label matters most: it is the
only description a screen reader announces for the send button, so
"Send command" stays exactly as it is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Update expectations for the penguin persona
commitResults.messageBody:
The JUnit and regression suites assert Nori's console output as exact
strings, so every message rewritten for the penguin persona now fails
its assertion.

These suites are the only automated check that the messages a user sees
are the messages the code intends, so leaving them stale would remove
that check rather than merely delay it.

Let's update each expected string to the new wording.

The assertions stay exact rather than relaxing to a substring match,
because the wording itself is what these tests protect; a typo in a
user-facing message should fail the build.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Update UI test plan for the penguin persona
commitResults.messageBody:
The UI test plan records a complete console session for each of its 17
cases, including every response Nori prints. Rewriting the messages
leaves all 17 expected output blocks stale.

The plan is the source of truth for scripted UI testing, and its runner
stops at the first mismatch. A stale plan therefore fails on case one
and hides any real regression behind the wording change.

Let's rewrite every expected output block to the new messages.

Each block is taken from an actual run and compared case by case, so the
plan still records what Nori does rather than what it ought to do. The
inputs and aims are untouched; only the expected text moves.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix: Punctuate every Javadoc tag description
commitResults.messageBody:
None of the 255 @param, @return and @throws descriptions across the code
base end with a full stop.

The Java coding standard asks for punctuation behind each parameter
description. Reviewers on the iP pull request flagged it in Command,
Event, Task and TaskList, and because Checkstyle does not check it the
same omission has spread to every file that has a Javadoc block.

Let's add the missing full stop to all 255 of them.

The fix lands in one commit across every file rather than file by file,
because a convention this mechanical is only useful once it holds
everywhere. A partial fix would leave the next reader unsure which of
the two forms the project intends.

Descriptions are otherwise untouched: no tag description spans more than
one line, so nothing needs rewrapping and no line crosses the 110
character soft limit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix: Remove ambiguity from task rendering Javadoc
commitResults.messageBody:
Task.getStatusIcon documents its result as {@code "X"} when complete,
otherwise "a space", and the four toString methods describe their output
with angle-bracket placeholders such as {@code [D][<status>]
<description> (by: MMM dd uuuu)}.

Neither form tells the reader what the method actually returns. "A
space" could be one character or padding of some unstated width, and
nothing says whether the angle brackets are literal output or stand-ins
for something else. Both were raised in review on the iP pull request.

Let's name the exact returned characters, drop the angle brackets, and
give every toString a worked example.

A worked example is used rather than more prose because each rendering
is short enough to show in full, and a reader comparing saved data or
console output against the documentation wants the literal text to
match against.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Rename DateRange fields to fromDate and toDate
commitResults.messageBody:
DateRange holds its two bounds in fields named from and to.

Read on their own the names give the direction of a bound but not what a
bound is, so anyone reading the class has to look at the declaration to
learn these hold dates rather than task numbers or list indices. A
reviewer on the iP pull request asked for the clearer names.

Let's rename the fields and the constructor parameters to fromDate and
toDate.

The getters keep the names getFrom and getTo. They are always called as
range.getFrom(), where the receiver already supplies the noun the name
would otherwise repeat, and renaming them would change a public API for
no gain in clarity.

No caller changes, because the rename touches only private state and
constructor parameter names.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Record the import groups Checkstyle enforces
commitResults.messageBody:
The Java standard requires a consistent import ordering but does not say
what the groups are, and docs/conventions/java.md repeats it at that
same level of detail.

That leaves undocumented the one case this project trips over.
Checkstyle sorts javafx.* and nori.* into the same catch-all group, so a
blank line between them is a violation, not an improvement. A reviewer
on the iP pull request suggested adding one, and the suggestion was
applied and then reverted once the build rejected it.

Let's write down the four groups from config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml,
and call out that javafx.* and nori.* share the last one.

The rule is recorded here rather than argued in a pull request comment
because the next reader has no way to derive it: the standard's prose
permits the split, and only the Checkstyle config forbids it. The
standard's own worked example agrees with the config, running javafx.*
and junit.* together, so the config is followed rather than changed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document the implicit constructors of three classes
commitResults.messageBody:
GuiUi, Main and MainWindow declare no constructor, so each gets an
implicit one. Running javadoc reports three warnings, one per class:
"use of default constructor, which does not provide a comment".

All three constructors are public API and all three are called: JavaFX
instantiates Main through its launcher, the FXML loader instantiates
MainWindow as the window's controller, and both Main and the tests
construct GuiUi directly. A reader of the generated documentation is
shown a constructor with nothing said about it.

Let's declare each constructor explicitly with a header comment naming
what constructs it.

Javadoc has no way to attach a comment to a constructor it generates, so
the constructor has to be written out to be documented. The bodies stay
empty, which leaves behaviour unchanged.

This clears the last three warnings, so the check named in
docs/conventions/java.md now reports zero.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-FullCommitMessage
commitResults.messageBody:
Nori's commit history carries subject lines only, and the conventions
behind those subjects exist only as links to se-education.org.

The A-FullCommitMessage increment asks for commit messages that explain
a change well enough to be judged without reading the diff. That is hard
to hold to when the rules are four web pages away, and the two reviews
on this pull request found the same gap in the code: Javadoc tag
descriptions missing their full stops, and return values described too
loosely to be unambiguous.

Let's merge the branch, which checks the SE-EDU guides into
docs/conventions, rewrites Nori's messages in a single penguin persona,
and clears the review findings.

Each of the 11 commits carries a full body, so the branch also serves as
the worked example the increment asks for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Verify the release JAR bundles JavaFX
commitResults.messageBody:
The release checklist asks for the JAR to be launched by hand from an
empty folder, and nothing else checks the artifact.

A JAR built without JavaFX bundled passes every other check this project
has. It compiles, the JUnit and UI suites pass against the source tree,
and it even runs from the console, because the console interface never
loads a JavaFX class. It fails only when a user opens the window on a
machine with no JavaFX installed, which is every machine a release
targets. The v0.1 artifact shipped at 35 KB for this reason.

Let's add test/jar_release_test.py, which verifies the built artifact
rather than the source: its size against a 5 MB floor, its Main-Class,
the JavaFX classes and native libraries inside it, and a real console
session run from a folder holding only the JAR.

Checking the built artifact is the point. Every existing suite runs
against src, so none of them can see a packaging fault; this one opens
the JAR and runs it.

The session case adds two tasks, exits, and relaunches to confirm the
saved data folder is read back, so a broken shading of resources or of
the storage path fails here rather than in a user's hands.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-FullCommitMessage
Build: Enable assertions when Nori runs
commitResults.messageBody:
Java evaluates an assert statement only when a launch passes -ea, so an
assertion added to the code would never be checked during development.

Nori is about to use assertions to state the assumptions its internal
methods rely on. Those statements are only worth writing if a developer
launch actually evaluates them.

Let's pass -ea through the application plugin's default JVM arguments.

Setting it on the application block covers `gradlew run` and the
generated start scripts in one place, and leaves the released JAR
unaffected, so end users keep running Nori with assertions disabled as
is standard for production.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Assert parser and command assumptions
commitResults.messageBody:
The parser trims a command line and matches its keyword before handing
the rest to the command factory, and the factory then trusts that every
recognised command type has a command class behind it. The commands that
change the task list also trust that a failed save can be undone by
removing the last task or reinserting at the index just vacated.

None of that is written down. A future change that breaks one of these
agreements surfaces far from its cause, as a string index error or as a
silent "I do not understand that command".

Let's state each assumption as an assertion at the point that relies on
it, with a message naming what establishes it.

Assertions rather than exceptions are right here: each one is an
agreement between Nori's own methods, not a check on what a user typed.
Everything a user can get wrong keeps its NoriException message, so
behaviour for a released build is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Assert task list and date range assumptions
commitResults.messageBody:
A date range reaches the task list already validated: the parser refuses
a range whose end date precedes its start, so DateRange, Deadline and
Event all compare the two bounds without rechecking their order. The
task list's own matching helper carries a second unwritten rule, that
exactly one of its two search arguments is supplied, and its heading
helper is called only when a search found something.

Those rules hold today by convention alone. Breaking one gives a wrong
answer rather than an error: a reversed range silently matches nothing,
and passing both search arguments quietly searches by date only.

Let's state each of them as an assertion in the method that depends on
it, naming the caller that establishes it.

The order check belongs in DateRange as well as in the two occurrence
methods, because each is a separate entry point that would otherwise
have to trust an argument it never sees built.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Assert session, storage and display assumptions
commitResults.messageBody:
Three more assumptions hold across Nori without being written down. A
session reports either a loading error or a loading notice but never
both, and getLoadingMessage returns only the first of them. A save
writes one line per task, which is what lets a reload restore the same
number of tasks. A response is printed only when there is something to
say, so the dividers always surround at least one line.

Each of these fails quietly rather than loudly. A second startup message
would simply disappear, a task lost during formatting would come back as
a shorter list, and an empty response would print two dividers around
nothing.

Let's assert all three where they are relied upon.

The storage assertion deliberately compares counts rather than checking
the lines themselves. It guards the invariant a reader depends on
without duplicating what the format methods already enforce.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Check assertions in every launched Nori session
commitResults.messageBody:
The regression suites start Nori in a separate java process, and a bare
java command leaves assertions disabled. Those suites drive Nori through
its whole command set, including corrupted storage files and malformed
input, which is exactly the traffic the new assertions must be measured
against.

Without -ea the assertions are dead code in the tests that exercise them
most, and an assertion accidentally written to fire on bad user input or
a damaged save file would pass unnoticed.

Let's pass -ea to every Nori process these suites launch.

That turns the suites into a check on the assertions themselves: one
that mistakes external data for a broken internal assumption now fails a
test instead of reaching a user.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Pull the shared task-adding step into a parent
commitResults.messageBody:
Three commands add a task: todo, deadline and event. All three need the
same sequence around it, saving the list and undoing the addition when
the save fails, and all three share it by calling a static method that
lives on TodoCommand.

That placement misleads a reader. The step has nothing to do with todos,
so a deadline reads as though it is doing something to a todo, and the
one class that happens to host the method cannot be understood or moved
on its own.

Let's pull the step up into a new AddTaskCommand parent that todo,
deadline and event extend, and call it as an inherited method.

Inheritance suits this better than a helper class: adding a task with a
rollback is behaviour these three commands have, not a service they
consult, and naming the parent states plainly what the three have in
common.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Give each command class its own source file
commitResults.messageBody:
Commands.java holds fourteen top-level classes in 479 lines: the command
factory, two abstract parents, and eleven commands.

A reader looking for what "delete" does has to scroll a file that also
defines everything else, and the Google Java Style Guide this project
falls back to asks for one top-level class per source file. Neither an
IDE's file list nor a directory listing tells anyone which commands
exist.

Let's move each class into a file named after it, leaving Commands.java
with the factory alone.

Nothing else changes: the classes keep their package-private visibility,
so the factory stays the only way into them from outside the package,
and each new file imports just the types its own class uses.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Separate dated-command checks from task creation
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding a deadline or an event mixes two jobs in one method. Each
execute() walks a chain of if/else branches that alternates between
finding fault with what the user typed and, in its final branch, calling
a second method that continues the same chain before building the task.

The two jobs read at different levels: one is about the shape of a
command line, the other about making a task. Spread over two methods and
a shared separator index, neither job can be read on its own, and the
order the faults are reported in is hard to see.

Let's have one method report the first fault it finds and let execute()
build the task once that method finds none.

The check method returns an Optional message, so a command with usable
details is stated by an empty result rather than by a null. Named
accessors for the description, the date and the times replace the index
arithmetic that both jobs previously shared.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Search the task list through one matching step
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list finds matching tasks in two private methods that differ
only in the test they apply. One of them serves both the date and the
date-range searches by taking both a date and a range and requiring the
caller to pass null for whichever it is not using.

The duplicated numbering loop has to stay in step in two places, and the
null argument makes a caller state which search it does not want. A
reader has to work out from the ternary inside the loop that passing
both values would silently search by date alone.

Let's number and collect matching tasks in one method that takes the
test to apply, and let each of the three searches supply its own test.

A Predicate keeps the numbering in a single place while leaving each
search's condition next to the method that needs it. The keyword search
still folds its keyword once, before the loop, rather than once per task.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Name the parts of a stored task line
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage writes and reads its own file format with the format spelled out
as literals: the type codes "T", "D" and "E", the completion statuses
"1" and "0", field positions 0 to 4, and line lengths 3, 4 and 5. The
separator is a named constant when a line is written but a hand-escaped
regular expression when one is read.

Anyone changing the format has to find every literal and know which 3
means "a to-do has three fields" and which means "a line needs at least
three fields". A reader of taskParts[3] cannot tell a due date from an
event's start without counting fields elsewhere in the method.

Let's give every part of the format a name, derive the reading
separator from the writing one, and move the per-type construction into
a createTask method of its own.

parseTask is then about what any stored line must have, and createTask
about what each task type looks like, so the length and index checks for
one type sit together instead of being spread down an if/else chain.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Give the unreadable-storage message one home
commitResults.messageBody:
Four places in Storage report a stored line that cannot be turned back
into a task, and each spells the message out in full.

The four copies are what a user sees, so they have to stay identical. A
reworded copy would leave a user meeting two different explanations of
the same problem depending on which check happened to catch the file.

Let's state the message once as a constant and refer to it from all four.

Deadline.fromStorage keeps its own copy of the wording. Sharing the
constant would make the task package depend on the storage package for
a string, which is a worse trade than the one repetition it removes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Pin the answer to every malformed deadline and event
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and event commands answer thirteen distinct faults with
thirteen distinct corrections, and the refactoring that separated
checking from creating moved every one of them. Only four of the
thirteen were covered anywhere.

Which correction a user gets is the whole value of these commands when
they type something wrong, and the order the checks run in decides
which correction wins when a line is wrong in more than one way.

Let's cover each fault, each of the two commands' successful cases, and
the whitespace-only inputs that reveal which check catches them.

The tests go through Nori and GuiUi rather than the command classes so
they pin what a user sees, not how the check is currently arranged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Drop the checks a trimmed command can never fail
commitResults.messageBody:
Both dated commands check twice for a missing description and twice for
a missing date: once for a separator sitting at the edge of the line,
and once for text either side of the separator turning out to be blank.
Each pair answers the same fault with different words.

The second check of each pair can never run. The parser hands a command
its details already trimmed, so text before the first separator is blank
only when the line starts with the separator, and text after the last
separator is blank only when the line ends with one. Both of those are
caught by the first check of the pair. Four corrections were therefore
written for users who cannot receive them, and a reader comparing the
two wordings has no way to tell which one is live.

Let's delete the four unreachable checks.

The suites cover all thirteen faults, including whitespace-only input,
and answer each one exactly as before.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Select matching tasks with a stream
commitResults.messageBody:
Both task searches walk the list with an index loop that does three
things at once: it counts, it decides whether a task matches, and it
builds the line shown for a match. The numbering expression is written
out twice, once in each loop.

A reader has to separate the counting from the matching before either
can be judged, and the two copies of the numbering have to be kept in
step by hand.

Let's express both searches as a stream over the task positions, with a
filter for the matching and a shared method for the numbered line.

An IntStream over positions rather than a stream of tasks is what keeps
a task's number in the full list available, which is the number a user
types into mark, unmark or delete. The result is collected with toList,
so a caller cannot alter a search result it only reads.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Assemble a response's lines with a stream
commitResults.messageBody:
Two methods build the array of lines a response is made of, and both do
it by hand: they size an array one larger than the content, place the
heading at position zero, and copy the rest across with an index that
has to be offset by one every time it is used.

The off-by-one offset is repeated four times between the two methods,
and the plain list of tasks is built twice in slightly different ways
even though a full listing is just a search that matched everything.

Let's concatenate the heading with the task lines, and have the full
listing reuse the same heading step as every other listing.

Streaming states the shape of a response directly, a heading followed by
its lines, instead of leaving a reader to reconstruct that shape from
array indices.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Recognize a command keyword with a stream
commitResults.messageBody:
Finding which command a line begins with is a search over the command
types, but it is written as a loop that computes two match conditions
into local variables, returns from inside the loop on the first hit, and
falls through to a lone return null at the end.

The search and the rule it searches by are tangled together, so neither
can be read without the other, and the loop's early return hides that
the first matching type is the one that wins.

Let's stream the command types, filter them by a named rule, and take
the first match.

Naming the rule as its own method also puts the exception for bye, which
takes no details and so must match the whole line, next to the ordinary
keyword rule it is an exception to.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refactor: Test a whole-number literal with a stream
commitResults.messageBody:
Deciding whether a rejected task number was a plain run of digits, and
so a number too large to hold rather than a typo, is done with a loop
that inspects one character at a time and returns false from inside on
the first non-digit.

What the loop asks is whether every character is a digit, but that
question is only visible after reading the loop's exit conditions and
its inverted test.

Let's ask it directly, of the characters after any leading sign.

The sign is still handled separately, because it is the one position
where a non-digit is allowed, and a bare sign with nothing after it
still has to be rejected before the digits are examined.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Show the build status in the README
commitResults.messageBody:
Continuous integration now runs every check on three operating systems,
but its result is only visible to someone who opens the Actions tab.

Anyone arriving at the repository, including a marker, should be able to
see at a glance whether master currently builds and passes its checks.

Let's put the workflow's status badge at the top of the README, linked
to the runs it summarises.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CI
Merge master into branch-A-Assertions
Merge master into branch-A-CodeQuality
Merge master into branch-A-Streams
Merge branch-A-Assertions
Merge master into branch-A-CodeQuality
commitResults.messageBody:
Master gained the A-Assertions increment, which added assertions to the
same command classes this branch moved into files of their own and to
the task-list search this branch replaced.

Resolved as follows.

The command classes keep their own files. The two assertions master
added inside them move with the code they describe: the one about a
newly added task being last now sits in AddTaskCommand, which owns that
step, and the one about a deleted task's index in DeleteCommand.

The task list keeps its single matching step. Master's assertion that
exactly one of a date and a date range is supplied is dropped, because
the two-argument method it described no longer exists; the assertion
that a range listing is given a range is kept.

Two cases in DatedTaskInputTest sent a command line with trailing
spaces, which no user interface can produce, and master's new assertion
that a parsed line is trimmed rightly rejected them. One duplicated an
existing case and is removed; the other now ends at the separator, which
is the reachable input it was meant to describe.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge master into branch-A-Streams
commitResults.messageBody:
Master gained the A-Assertions increment, which added assertions to the
two task-list methods this branch rewrote as streams.

Both assertions still hold and are kept, ahead of the stream they now
guard: a search is still by a single date or by a range and never both,
and a heading is still added only when a search matched something.

The parser merged without conflict; the assertions it gained apply to
the input handling around the keyword lookup, not to the lookup itself.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CodeQuality
Merge master into branch-A-Streams
commitResults.messageBody:
Master gained the A-CodeQuality increment, which had already replaced
the task list's two near identical search loops with one method taking
the test to apply. This branch had instead rewritten the same two loops
as streams, keeping the two-argument shape.

The two changes improve different halves of the same method, so the
resolution keeps both: one search method taking a Predicate, with its
body expressed as a stream over the task positions.

The assertion that exactly one of a date and a range is supplied goes
with the two-argument method it described. The keyword search keeps
master's containsKeyword helper, and this branch's numbering helper
stays, because both the search and the full listing use it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Streams
Feat: Read a clock time from an event's start details
commitResults.messageBody:
An event keeps its start and end exactly as the user typed them, and only
a date is ever parsed out of that text. The hour in "2026-09-01 0900" is
therefore stored, shown and then ignored.

A schedule has to put a day's events in the order they happen, so
something has to turn that written hour into a time it can sort by.
Nothing does.

Let's read the first clock time out of an event's start details, and
report which time an event starts at on a given date.

Reading the time back out of text the user already types keeps the saved
file format untouched, so every existing save file still loads and the
deadline and event commands keep their syntax. The alternative, storing a
time of its own, would have changed both.

The times accepted are the ones this app's own examples use: 0900, 9:00,
9.30, 2pm, 2:30 PM, 9 a.m. An event counts as timed on a date only when
its start details name that date, because the hour a multi-day event
began at says nothing about the days after it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Cover clock times in event start details
commitResults.messageBody:
Reading a time out of free-form text is guesswork constrained by rules,
and the rules are only worth having if the guesses are pinned down.

Two kinds of mistake matter. Reading a time that is not there would put
an event at an invented hour: a year's four digits look exactly like a
24-hour time, and 2400 or 9:60 look nearly like one. Missing a time that
is there would quietly drop an event out of a schedule's ordering.

Let's cover every form the reader accepts, every near miss it must
reject, and the cases where a date sits beside the time it must find.

The Event tests cover the rule on top of those: a start time counts on
the day the start names and on no other, so a multi-day event is untimed
on its later days.

commitResults.messageTitle: Feat: Show one day's tasks as a schedule
commitResults.messageBody:
Nori can filter a day but it cannot lay one out. The "on" command prints
the deadlines and events falling on a date in whatever order they were
added, so a user reading it still has to work out what happens first.

Seeing a day in the order it will actually run is the point of keeping
dated tasks at all, and it is the one view a task list of this shape
cannot already give.

Let's add a "schedule" command that lays a date out: the events that
start at a known time on it, earliest first, then the events running over
it without a time of their own, then the deadlines falling due, then
every to-do.

To-dos are included because they have no date and so suit any day, and
they are kept in a section of their own so they never crowd out what the
day is actually committed to. Sections with nothing in them are dropped
rather than printed empty. Rows carry the numbers the full list uses, so
a number read off a schedule works with mark, unmark and delete, exactly
as one read off "find" already does.

A bare "schedule" means today, which is the question a user most often
has and which nothing in Nori could previously answer. "on" is left
untouched: it still does its own smaller job for anyone relying on it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test: Cover the schedule command end to end
commitResults.messageBody:
A schedule is almost all presentation: which section a task lands in,
what order the timed ones come out in, and how the rows line up. None of
that is checked by the tests the other commands brought with them.

The ordering is the part most likely to break silently. A schedule that
loses its sort still prints every task, still numbers them correctly and
still looks right at a glance, so nothing but an explicit check on the
order would catch it.

Let's cover the day from three sides: the task list's own lines, whole
commands run through Nori, and a real Nori process reading a session.

The command tests pin every section boundary, the two multi-day cases
that decide whether an event is timed, the ordering when it disagrees
with task-list order, ties, an unreadable date, and that a number read
off a schedule still marks the right task. The regression case asserts
the order of the sections as well as their contents, since containment
alone cannot tell a sorted day from an unsorted one.

The test plan gains the same session as a console case, and its help
case takes on the two new commands and the tip about times.

commitResults.messageTitle: Docs: Document the schedule command in the user guide
commitResults.messageBody:
The user guide is still the template it shipped as, so the one command
whose output a reader cannot predict from its name has nothing written
about it anywhere outside the app.

A schedule needs explaining more than the other commands do. Which
section a task lands in follows from rules a user cannot see, and the
ordering only works if a time was written into an event's /from, which
nothing about the deadline or event syntax suggests.

Let's document the sections, the times the /from field is read for, and
what happens when a date cannot be read.

The rest of the guide stays as it is. Filling it in is the user-guide
increment's job, and half-completing it here would leave a reader unsure
which parts had been written and which were still placeholders.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-B-ViewSchedules
